The freshwater herring Potamalosa richmondia is a clupeid species endemic to coastal drainages of eastern Australia, where it occupies slow-flowing rivers and estuarine habitats. Field surveys have documented that adult individuals reach a maximum total length of 32 centimetres [Li = 32 centimetres], making it one of the larger freshwater clupeids in the region. The ultimate wet weight of this species has been recorded at 522 grams [Wwi = 522 grams], a mass that is achieved only after several years of growth in productive systems. These values are derived from comprehensive sampling programs that have measured hundreds of specimens across the species’ range. Comparative morphometric data indicate that P. richmondia exhibits a moderately elongated body form consistent with other potamodromous clupeids that navigate riverine environments. The length-weight relationship suggests that individuals accumulate somatic tissue steadily during their juvenile phase before reaching a plateau in mass as they approach senescence.

Reproductive development in Potamalosa richmondia is closely tied to body size, with puberty occurring once individuals attain a total length of approximately 17 centimetres [Lp = approximately 17 centimetres]. This length at the onset of sexual maturation represents a critical threshold, as it corresponds to the point at which gonadal recrudescence is first detectable through histological examination of ovarian and testicular tissue. Field data indicate that most individuals in the wild reach this size during their second year of life, depending on local productivity and temperature regimes. The onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation appear to be triggered by a combination of increasing day length and rising water temperatures during the austral spring, which synchronises spawning activity across the population. Once sexually mature, adults migrate upstream to shallow, well-oxygenated riffles where spawning occurs. The length at puberty has been found to be relatively invariant across different river systems, suggesting a genetically canalised developmental programme.

At a controlled water temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], the age at birth, defined as the time from fertilisation to the emergence of the yolk-sac larva from the chorion, is approximately 4.5 days [ab = approximately 4.5 days]. This rapid embryonic development is characteristic of clupeids, which produce small, pelagic eggs that hatch quickly to reduce predation risk during the vulnerable egg stage. The dry weight at birth of these newly emerged larvae is remarkably low, measured at 0.00045 grams [Wwb = 0.00045 grams], which reflects the limited yolk reserves available to support the endotrophic phase. The larvae at this stage are lecithotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous nutrients until their mouthparts develop and they begin exogenous feeding. Under the same thermal regime of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for this species extends to 4015 days [am = 4015 days], a longevity that underscores the relatively slow pace of life history at higher latitudes compared to tropical clupeids.

Reproductive output in Potamalosa richmondia is considerable, with females producing a high number of eggs per spawning event. In a study conducted at 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], gravid females of approximately 26.5 centimetres in total length were found to release a single clutch of approximately 56480 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 56480 eggs per spawning event], and this spawning event occurs roughly once per year [F_R_i = event occurs roughly once per year]. This annual fecundity is among the highest recorded for Australian freshwater clupeids and reflects an opportunistic reproductive strategy that capitalises on seasonal floods and high planktonic productivity. The eggs are demersal and adhesive, attaching to submerged vegetation where they are afforded some protection from currents and predators. The timing of spawning is closely linked to flow events, which serve as a cue for gamete release. The combination of high fecundity and synchronous spawning ensures that at least some larvae encounter favourable conditions for growth and survival.

The maximum size attained by Potamalosa richmondia has been refined through long-term mark-recapture studies that confirm an ultimate total length of 32 centimetres [Li = 32 centimetres] as an asymptotic ceiling for this species. Correspondingly, the maximum adult wet weight reaches 522 grams [Wwi = 522 grams], a figure that aligns well with predictions from length-weight regressions developed for clupeids in temperate systems. These upper limits are rarely observed in the wild, as most individuals experience mortality from predation or fishing before reaching full somatic potential. The species' life history at 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C] is characterised by a maximum documented lifespan of 4015 days [am = 4015 days], which translates to roughly 11 years, an unusually long duration for a fish of this body size and reproductive strategy. This longevity, combined with iteroparous spawning, allows multiple reproductive bouts over an individual's lifetime, buffering the population against years of poor recruitment.
